issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. Generic sensory cues can fit disaster trauma, but snakes and babies are highly specific cues with no clear link to a natural disaster and, taken together with body odour, suggest unrelated trigger themes rather than a single trauma network.

Within the overall profile, the memory/appraisal content is also mismatched. 'Intense shame on recall' usually implies a strong negative appraisal/self-evaluative theme, yet no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is formulation-wise disconnected. For a natural disaster survivor, shame can occur, but as the only explicit meaning-based memory item it sits awkwardly with otherwise cue-driven fragmented recall and no corresponding appraisal content.

'Babies' as an auditory trigger is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma in this profile unless there is specific undisclosed trauma content involving infants; the other triggers (loud noises, sweat/body odour) are more disaster-congruent, so this item stands out as clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers mainly with memory and only minimally with maladaptive strategies, and the other selected items suggest intrusive sensory recall rather than an anger/interpersonal-dysregulation pattern. This coping item appears to target a symptom style not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' is likewise poorly supported by the rest of the profile. With no threat or negative appraisal content selected and memory items focused on fragmentation/triggered recall, this strategy lacks a clear cognitive-affective anchor in the chosen profile and is difficult to connect specifically to natural-disaster PTSD here.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, sweat/body odour and alcohol smell are hard to link plausibly as primary trauma reminders unless there is additional disaster-specific context (e.g., shelter crowding, intoxicated bystanders). Loud noises fit, but these two olfactory triggers are clinically difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but as the only affective memory item here it is a poor fit with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes sensory triggering and fragmented involuntary recall rather than self-blame, humiliation, or morally charged memory content. This makes the memory node less coherent with the trauma type and the selected triggers/strategies.

Alcohol smell is a hard-to-explain trigger for a natural-disaster trauma in the absence of any matching trauma context or linked appraisal content; loud noise and smoke are coherent disaster-related cues, but alcohol odor stands out as clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but with no negative-appraisal content and no other memory material suggesting shame-linked actions or moral failure, this item is poorly supported and clinically discordant with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Using alcohol can occur nonspecifically, but paired with an alcohol-smell trigger it implies trauma meaning centered on alcohol-related cues that is not represented elsewhere in the disaster-based trigger or memory profile, reducing coherence.

vignette:
Daniel Morales, a 40-year-old Latino American surgeon, came to treatment after months of feeling on edge in ways that seemed to catch him off guard. The traumatic event he described reached back to a wildfire that swept through the neighborhood where he and his wife had been staying while visiting family. He still remembered the night as a sequence of broken pieces rather than a complete scene: the hard crack of something collapsing, the roar and popping of flames, the smell of smoke thickening in the air and then, later, the sharper burnt smell that seemed to cling to everything. He had tried to help relatives move quickly, but the memory he carried now was incomplete, composed of flashes - darkness lit by orange light, hurried footsteps, his own voice shouting directions, and then long gaps where he could not say exactly what happened. What stayed with him most was not only fear in the moment but the grief that now rose whenever his mind returned to that night, a heavy sense of loss that made him feel as if he were standing inside the event again, remembering not just danger but what had been taken from safety and normal life.

In the months that followed, Daniel found that certain experiences could bring the entire scene back without warning. A loud bang in the hospital corridor, a metal tray dropped suddenly in the operating suite, even the sharp slam of a door could make his body react before his mind caught up. At those moments he would feel the wildfire memory arrive all at once, vivid and immediate, as though the present had been torn open and replaced by that night. Smoke or fire smell had an even more specific power over him. Walking past a restaurant kitchen, passing a building with a furnace odor, or entering a room where something had been overheated could make him tense instantly, and the burnt smell in particular would stop him in his tracks. He became alert to these cues in a way others around him did not notice, scanning the environment for traces of heat, smoke, or anything that suggested something might be burning. What frightened him most was how little warning he seemed to get; something in the air or a sudden noise could pull him straight back into the disaster before he had a chance to steady himself.

As the weeks turned into months, Daniel began arranging his life around the hope of avoiding that jolt of remembering. After long shifts he often tried to distract himself by immersing in whatever was available - scrolling on his phone, putting on television for background noise, staying busy with tasks that did not require him to sit still with his thoughts. He also noticed that he drank alcohol more often than he had before, sometimes using it at the end of the day to blunt the tension he carried home from the hospital. At times he relied on medication or other substances he had access to, telling himself he just needed to get through the night and be ready for the next day's operating schedule. He was ashamed of how much effort it took to push away the memory, and there were evenings when he sought relief through sexual fantasies or activities, not as a way of connecting but as a private means of releasing pressure and switching off the distress that had built up in him. These habits did not erase the memory, but they became part of the way he managed each day, especially after exhausting shifts when he felt least able to tolerate another unwanted surge of recollection.

At work, Daniel remained outwardly functional, but his experience of the hospital changed. He was still doing surgery, still moving through the routine demands of his profession, yet he found himself more watchful in environments where loud noises were common and where anything that smelled burnt could become instantly disturbing. A smoke odor from equipment or a sudden clang in the operating area could leave him briefly unsettled, his attention pulled away from the task in front of him. At home, his wife noticed that he was more likely to retreat into distraction rather than talk about what had happened, and he carried the burden of knowing that even when he appeared composed, he was often managing the sudden return of a memory that felt fragmented and overwhelming. He sought help now because the reminders had become too frequent and too intrusive to ignore, and because he was tired of living as though any loud sound or trace of smoke might drop him back into that night. What he hoped for was not to forget the wildfire, but to be able to remember it without being overtaken by grief and without having to organize his days around the next unexpected reminder.
